In our paper we suggest just taking all of these duplicate sequences that have been identified and completely striking them from the dataset. This somewhat breaks the flow of text, for example if previously had an example "Alice wanted to go to the store" and we deduplicated at the level of 10 characters, we might completely strike " to go to the " and be left with "Alice wantedstore". In practice we have found this doesn't break the language model because we remove relatively little text, and so these breaks don't cause harm.

We also release the document clusters resulting from running NearDup deduplication on C4, RealNews, LM1B, and Wiki-4B-en. This is not an officially supported Google product. When datasets are created by scraping raw text from the Internet, this will often result in the same sequences being repeated multiple times (e.g., we find a single 50 word sequence that is repeated in the C4 dataset 60,000 times). Training models on deduplicated datasets is faster (because they see fewer total examples) and experimentally results in models with similar or better perplexity to models trained on data that hasn't been deduplicated.
Moreover, language models are less likely to exhibit memorization when their training data has been well-deduplicated.
